title: Footers that help
metaTitle: A footer for people who are lost
excerpt: The footer is for people who did not find their path. Repeat the action, the legal facts, and a few real destinations. Leave the archive of every page out.
alt: A white modernist building with stacked cubic volumes and tall windows against a pale sky, a clear base under the structure for an article about footers that still help.
caption: A building with a readable base, not a pile of every room. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs in a website footer?
faqs.answer: Repeat the main action, the legal name and policies, and a few destinations people still need, such as contact, the offer, and docs or status if those pages are real. A short line on who you are helps someone who landed mid-site. The footer is a rescue, not a second sitemap of every URL you have published.

faqs.question: Should the footer change on every page?
faqs.answer: The core should stay stable so people learn where the action and the policies live. A section can add a local link, such as a changelog inside docs, without removing the way back to the offer. A footer that is a different puzzle on every template fails at the moment they needed a habit.

faqs.question: Where should legal links go?
faqs.answer: Put privacy, terms, and the company identity in the footer, in readable type, with real names on the links. They should be on the pages where you collect information. Tiny grey text that cannot be tapped is not a kindness. It fails the person who actually wants to read the policy.

markdown:
Website footer design is a rescue for the person who did not find their path. They scrolled, or they landed in the middle of the site, and the header is gone. Repeat the action. Put the legal facts where they can be read. Offer a few real destinations. Leave the archive of every page you have ever made out of this strip.

A footer that helps is short enough to scan and stable enough to become a habit. It should sound like the same company as the first screen. It is the last competent moment on the page.

## Who the footer is for

Assume they are slightly lost, not that they are admiring the grid. They want the thing the page promised, or they want to know the company is real, or they want a policy before they type an email. Serve those jobs in that order. The action first, because some of them are ready and the header has scrolled away. Then a plain statement of who you are. Then the policies and the extra doors.

The person who reaches the footer has often given the page more time than a casual bounce. Do not spend that attention on a second hero, and do not cover the links with a newsletter layer. Give them the action they already saw, in the same words. If the header said to book a thirty-minute intro, the footer should not switch to a vaguer invitation. Same verb, same expectation.

[People-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a reader can tell the purpose of a site and who stands behind it. The footer is a natural place for the second answer: the legal name, a place if that fact is useful, and a way to reach a human. A row of social icons with no name is a set of exits. It is not an identity. Put the name in text.

## A few destinations, chosen on purpose

Pick links a lost person can use.

- The offer, in the buyer's language.
- Proof, if the work is how you are judged.
- The same way to talk that the header uses.
- Docs or status, when those pages are real.
- Privacy, terms, and any policy you actually maintain.

Five to eight links is a scan. Thirty is a dump, and dumps hide the one link they needed. If the docs are large, link to the docs home, not to every article. If you have a journal, link to the journal, not to the last forty posts. Archives belong on archive pages. The footer is an index of doors, not the building.

Name the links the way the pages are named. If the page title says the job, the footer should use that job. A cute shortening that does not match the heading makes people think they took a wrong turn. The footer is often how they confirm they are in the right place. Match it.

Group the links when you have more than a handful. Product. Company. Policies. The labels should be dull and true. "Explore" is not a group. It is a shrug. You are not writing a second homepage. You are labeling doors so a tired person can choose.

Retire links that 404, that open empty campaigns, or that exist so a stakeholder's page is "in the footer." Every dead link taxes the live ones. Check them when you ship, and check them when a page is removed. A smaller true list is the maintenance. Addition is how this strip rots.

## Repeat the action without a new personality

One primary action. If an address is a real secondary path, and a person reads it, put it in text they can copy. Do not add a second equal button that splits the decision the page just made. Header and footer should agree about what happens next.

A line under the action can say the limit. Thirty minutes. Fit, the shape of the work, and whether a proposal is worth writing. The person who scrolled is often the person who was unsure. A limit makes the yes easier. It also keeps the footer from sounding like a different sales motion than the intro.

Match the page. A product page with a signup should repeat the signup, not detour into a brand essay. An article can point at the intro, and the article's own next link can stay in the body. The footer should not fight that ending. They can share a door. They should not offer two puzzles.

On a phone the action is a button a thumb can hit, near the top of the footer, before the legal block. Stack the groups. Do not ask someone to parse four columns of tiny type to find the only thing they came to do. The fine print matters, and it should follow the rescue, not bury it.

## Legal facts, in type you can read

Privacy and terms are part of help. People look for them when they are about to trust you with an address or a payment. Put them on every page, including forms. The link text should say what they are. A logo is not a policy. "Legal" as a single mystery link is weaker than naming the documents.

[The W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the public standard for text people can perceive and controls they can operate. Footer type in light grey on a slightly different grey fails in daylight, and it fails the spirit of the policy you linked. Use a contrast you would accept in a paragraph. Small can still be readable. Illegible cannot. The hit area has to be tappable. A line of text that only works with a precise cursor is a policy hidden in plain sight.

Spell the company name as it appears on the terms. A nickname in the footer and a different entity on the policy is a seam at a bad moment. Copyright lines are fine. A badge you did not earn, or a client logo you cannot show, is not. People look here for the unglamorous truth. Stock the strip with truth.

Link status if you have a status page that loads when the product does not. Link a security contact if you publish one. These are doors for a specific kind of lost. Omit them when they are not real. A status link that 404s during a calm week will be remembered during a bad one.

## Keep the habit, and allow a local extra

The core should be stable across the marketing site. People learn that the action repeats at the bottom and that policies live there. Rebuilding the footer for every template throws away the learning. Change a link when a destination changes. Do not change the pattern because one page wanted to feel special.

Docs can add a local link, such as the changelog, without deleting the way home. A product shell can be smaller: status, docs, account. Do not paste the entire marketing footer into the app. The jobs differ. The identity should still match, so a jump from the product to a policy does not feel like a different company. Same name, same type, a shorter list.

A language switch belongs here only if the languages exist. A control that promises a translation you have not written is a broken door. If you have one language, skip the control. Honesty is quieter and more useful. If you do offer a theme or a contrast choice, keep it secondary to the action. The preference is a neighbor. The rescue still leads.

Reduced motion is mostly a system setting, not a footer toy. If a control lives here, it should be findable again on the next page, in the same place. A one-off toggle that disappears on the next template is a trick. Stability is the point of putting anything in this strip at all.

## What to leave in the page, not in the footer

Leave the full history out. Old campaigns, expired events, every tag, every author. Those URLs can exist. They do not all need a permanent seat. Clutter lowers the odds of finding privacy or the call, which are the links with a job today. When you are unsure, delete. You can add a link back when someone actually needs it.

Leave keyword variants out. Three links that are the same page in different synonyms help neither a person nor a careful reading of what a site is for. [Helpful pages](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) are the test: would someone who is lost be glad this is here. If the gladness is only internal, remove it. The footer is a utility. Utilities that advertise themselves get ignored.

Leave autoplay, stock scenes, and a museum of logos for other parts of the page, if they belong anywhere. A logo row with permission and a sentence can sit near proof, higher up. The footer is a poor museum and a good index. Do not make people scroll through a brand film to reach the privacy link. That is the opposite of a rescue.

## Build it as part of the page, not an afterthought

In the document, the footer is a landmark at the end, present in the HTML, not injected so late that the page jumps when it arrives. A strip that pops in and shifts the content punishes the person about to tap. Reserve the space. One component, so a policy URL changes everywhere when it changes once. Copy-pasted footers drift, and drift is how an old campaign outlives the offer.

On a Hanabi site that component shares type and color with the header, in React and Tailwind, with real anchors. The repository the client owns should show where the list lives, so an edit is a change, not a ticket into a layout trapped as an image. A footer inside a picture cannot be read by a search, a keyboard, or a person who zooms. It looks like a finish and behaves like a wall.

Review it last, on a phone, from a page that is not the home page. Can you say what to do next. Can you find privacy. Can you tell the company's name. If any answer is no, remove links until the answers are yes. The review is subtraction. The launch screenshot will look calmer, and the person who is lost will have a chance.

A missing URL is a harder case than a long page. The footer can still help, and the missing page has to offer a way forward of its own. [A 404 page that keeps the visit](/blog/a-404-page-that-keeps-the-visit) is that next piece. Read it so the dead end and the footer tell one story: an action, a real destination, and a name.
